Hatchlings of the Red-legged kittiwake (Rissa brevirostris) emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after a developmental period of 27 days [ab = 27 days], a duration that reflects the relatively rapid embryonic growth typical of cliff-nesting alcids exposed to cool maritime climates. At the moment of hatching, these semi-precocial chicks weigh approximately 30 grams [Wwb = approximately 30 grams], a modest birth mass that is somewhat lower than that of its better-studied congener, the black-legged kittiwake (Rissa tridactyla). This lower neonatal mass may be an adaptation to the energetic constraints of provisioning in the more remote and storm-prone Bering Sea colonies where this species breeds. The downy chicks are brooded intensively during the first few days, with parents alternating between guarding and foraging trips, ensuring the hatchling receives sufficient warmth and protection from predation.

Under the active metabolic conditions of the nesting cycle, typically associated with a body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], young kittiwakes fledge the nest after approximately 32 days since birth [tx = approximately 32 days since birth]. This fledging period is notably short for a gull of this size and likely reflects selective pressure to depart the narrow cliff ledges before terrestrial predators or intraspecific competition become intense. During the nestling stage, the developing chick grows rapidly, shedding its initial down for juvenile plumage, and begins to exercise its wings vigorously on the ledge in the days leading up to fledging. The success of this critical developmental transition depends heavily on consistent parental provisioning; chicks that receive insufficient food may delay fledging or achieve a poorer body condition at independence.

Sexual maturation in this species, measured under the same thermal regime of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], is estimated to occur at approximately 96 days since birth [tp = approximately 96 days since birth]. This relatively early attainment of gonadal maturity, when compared to larger gulls, allows young birds to begin scouting for potential breeding sites and establishing pair bonds during their first summer, even though they do not typically engage in nesting until later. The onset of puberty is marked by the development of the characteristic red legs and the subtle changes in bill coloration that distinguish adults from immatures. First-year birds often return to the natal colony, engaging in courtship displays and ritualized feeding behaviors that strengthen pair formation, though actual breeding is postponed.

First reproduction, or the first successful brood, generally occurs at 4 years since birth [tR = 4 years since birth] under a metabolic body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], a delay that reflects the time required to secure a high-quality nesting territory on the crowded volcanic cliffs of the Pribilof Islands and other core breeding sites. This deferred breeding is typical of long-lived seabirds and allows individuals to accumulate experience in foraging efficiency and predator avoidance before committing to the substantial energetic costs of egg production and chick rearing. Under these thermal conditions, females typically lay a single clutch per year, with each clutch containing 1 to 2 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 1 to 2 eggs] and typically approximately 1 to 2 successful clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1 to 2 successful clutches annually], a relatively low reproductive output compared to many other charadriiforms.

The maximum recorded lifespan for the Red-legged kittiwake, observed under field conditions at a metabolic body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], is approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years]. This impressive longevity is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high annual fecundity, a pattern common among pelagic seabirds that face unpredictable food resources in the Bering Sea ecosystem. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults ranges considerably, from approximately 325 to 510 grams, with a typical mean value near 480 grams [Wwi = 480 grams]. This adult mass places Rissa brevirostris as a medium-sized gull, somewhat smaller than the closely related Rissa tridactyla, a difference that may reduce absolute food requirements during the non-breeding season and confer an energetic advantage when foraging in the productive but variable shelf waters of the North Pacific.
